about: cURL Studio translates a pasted `curl` command into request code for JavaScript (fetch), Python (requests), Go (net/http), Java 11+ (HttpClient), C# (HttpClient), Rust (reqwest, blocking) and PHP (cURL). It also goes the other way: paste a snippet that follows one of those literal request patterns and get the equivalent `curl` command. The usual starting point is a command copied from API documentation or from the browser's network panel, which you then need inside an application.

The converter works by parsing, not by running anything. The input is tokenised with shell-style quoting rules, mapped to a small request model of method, URL, headers and body, validated, and then rendered by a per-language generator. Nothing is executed, no request is sent and no code you paste is evaluated. The README states that no network access, telemetry or third-party runtime dependency is used.

That design makes the tool predictable but narrow. It supports the options most API calls actually use and rejects the rest with a specific error rather than producing code that quietly behaves differently from your command. If a snippet comes out, the method, URL, headers and body in it are the ones you gave.

Before converting, you may want to tidy a JSON body in [JSON Tools](/json-tools/) or check a bearer token in [JWT Trust Lab](/jwt-tools/). Sensitive headers are kept in the output exactly as typed, so redact tokens before sharing a generated snippet.

features.title: Seven target languages
features.body: JavaScript fetch, Python requests, Go net/http, Java HttpClient, C# HttpClient, Rust reqwest and PHP cURL. Each is generated from the same request model so they stay consistent with each other.

features.title: Reverse conversion for literal requests
features.body: Snippets that match the generator's own request constructs can be turned back into cURL. Variables, computed expressions and unrelated libraries are rejected rather than guessed.

features.title: Realistic option coverage
features.body: Handles `-X`, `-H`, `-d`, `--data-raw`, `--data-binary`, `--data-urlencode`, `--json`, `--url`, `-A`, `-b`, `-u` and `-I`, including `--option=value` and attached forms such as `-XPOST`. Backslash line continuations are understood.

features.title: Helpful implied behaviour
features.body: A body without `-X` makes the method POST, as curl does. `--json` adds `Content-Type: application/json` if you did not set one, and `-u user:pass` becomes a Basic Authorization header.

features.title: Warnings for dropped options
features.body: Flags that do not translate to a snippet, such as `-L`, `-s`, `-k`, `--compressed` and `-i`, produce a visible warning instead of silently disappearing.

features.title: Input guards
features.body: Input is limited to 100,000 characters, bodies to 64 KiB, headers to 64, and only http and https URLs without embedded credentials are accepted.

reference.title: How a cURL command maps to a request, and what is rejected

blocks.text: The command must begin with `curl`. Single quotes keep everything literal, double quotes allow backslash escapes for backslash, double quote, dollar sign and backtick, and a backslash at the end of a line joins it with the next, which is how multi-line commands copied from documentation are written. A `#` that starts a word begins a comment.

Shell variables and substitutions are refused: `$TOKEN`, `${HOST}`, `$(date)` and backticks all cause an error asking for literal arguments. This matters because the converter cannot know what the shell would have expanded them to, and a wrong guess would give you code that sends a different request.

head: cURL option
Effect in the request model
rows: Adds a header; the first colon splits name from value
Appends to the body; several values are joined with `&`
Percent-encodes the value after the first `=`
Sets the body and a default JSON content type
Adds `Authorization: Basic` with Base64 of the UTF-8 value

items: `-d @file` and stdin references: the tool is text-only and cannot read files. `--data-raw` is exempt because it treats `@` literally.
`-G` or `--get`: moving data into the query string cannot be expressed faithfully in the snippet model.
Multiple URLs, unknown options and multipart form flags such as `-F`.
URLs that are not http or https, or that contain a username and password in the authority.
Header names that contain characters not allowed in HTTP tokens, and header values containing line breaks, which prevents header injection in the generated code.

blocks.text: Redirect following, TLS verification and compression are client settings, not part of the request. Because `-L`, `-k` and `--compressed` are only warned about, a Python or Go snippet may follow redirects or verify certificates differently from your command. Set those options in your HTTP client explicitly.

Generated strings are escaped for the target language: JSON-style quoting for most, and single-quoted escaping for PHP. Java uses the `java.net.http` client added in Java 11, so older runtimes need a different library. The Rust output uses the blocking reqwest API, which needs its blocking feature enabled in `Cargo.toml`. If you need typed models for the response, generate them from a sample in [POJO to Any](/pojo-to-any/).
Bodies are treated as text. A JSON body is sent as the exact characters you provided, so key order and spacing are preserved, and binary content is not supported.

example.title: Turn a documentation example into Python

blocks.text: Paste this command, which is typical of API documentation, and select Python (requests).

The output contains a requests call with the method POST, the URL, a headers dictionary with both headers and the JSON string as the body. Check three things before copying it: the method matches, the Authorization value is still the placeholder, and the body is exactly the JSON you intended.

Now change the command to use `-H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`. The converter stops with the message that shell variables are not supported. Replace `$TOKEN` with a literal value or a clear placeholder, convert, and then swap the placeholder for your environment lookup in code. Adding `-L` would produce the snippet plus a warning that redirect following is not preserved.

limits: Only a subset of cURL is supported. Multipart uploads, file bodies, `-G`, proxies, client certificates, cookies jars, retries and timeouts are not converted.
Reverse conversion recognises only the literal constructs this tool generates. It is not a code interpreter and will reject loops, variables and helper functions.
The converter does not send the request. To see the real response, run the generated code or the original command yourself.
Output contains the headers and tokens you pasted. Review it before sharing or committing it.
Generated code is a starting point: it has no error handling, retries, timeouts or response parsing.

faq.question: Why does it reject my command with a dollar sign?
faq.answer: Variables such as `$TOKEN` are expanded by the shell, and the tool cannot know their values. Replace them with literal text, convert, then substitute your own configuration lookup in the code.

faq.question: Why did my GET become a POST?
faq.answer: curl sends POST when a body is supplied with `-d` and no `-X`. The converter follows that rule. Add `-X GET` explicitly if you want a GET with a body.

faq.question: Does the tool call the API?
faq.answer: No. It only parses the text and generates code. No request is made and no data is sent anywhere.

faq.question: Are -L, -k and --compressed supported?
faq.answer: They are recognised and produce a warning, but they are not included in the generated snippet. Configure redirects, certificate verification and compression in your HTTP client.

faq.question: What about file uploads?
faq.answer: File and stdin bodies (`-d @file`) and multipart forms are not supported because the converter is text-only. Use your client library's multipart support directly.
